title: Fairness-Aware Multi-view Evidential Learning
one_liner: When a model learns from multiple data sources, it hands out unfair evidence to rare classes; this paper fixes it by watching the model's mistakes and then gently steering evidence allocation to be balanced.
lead: Imagine a doctor with reports from three different hospitals. The hospitals with more patients have louder voices, so rare diseases get less evidence. This paper finds that multi-view models have the same problem: they assign evidence (how much the data supports a class label) unfairly, giving rare classes short shrift. The fix is to watch how the model struggles during training, then use that history as a brake to keep evidence allocation fair.

problem.h2: Evidence gets captured by loud classes
paras: When a model learns from multiple views (different data sources, different sensors, different perspectives), it collects evidence for each possible class from each view separately. Evidence is just a number saying how much the data in that view supports that class.

The problem: real-world data is rarely balanced. Some classes have tons of examples, others have just a handful. Models tend to collect lots of evidence for the common classes and ignore the rare ones. This creates a lopsided, unreliable picture: the model is confident about common things but silently unsure about rare things.

A beginner might just mix the evidence together, assuming each view knows what it is doing. But garbage in means garbage out. If one view assigns evidence unfairly, averaging garbage still yields garbage.

callout.html: Evidence learning assigns more support to common classes and less to rare ones, breaking the model's uncertainty estimates.

steps.b: Collect raw evidence from each view
steps.text: Each neural network extracts how much each view supports each class label.
During training, log which samples the model got wrong and when.
Use the pattern of mistakes to estimate how much each class needs a boost, because classes that fail early are usually the ones the model is going to ignore.
Add a penalty to the loss if evidence variance across classes is unbalanced.
Check that different views agree; if one view is an outlier, pull it toward consensus.

paras: The paper changes one thing: how much confidence (evidence) each class receives during learning. Instead of collecting evidence blindly, the model now receives guidance on which classes need more support.

hidden.name: Fairness degree (class-wise evidence variance)
paras: Fairness degree is a single number that measures whether evidence is spread evenly across classes. If one class has tall evidence stacks and another has tiny ones, fairness is low. It is computed as the variance (how spread out the evidence values are) for each class, measured across views.

The paper uses this quantity as a penalty: it adds a cost to the loss function if classes have lopsided evidence spreads. By measuring fairness explicitly, the model learns to stop ignoring rare classes.

heat.caption: Darker means more evidence collected. Highlights show rare classes being starved.

reads.html: Fairness degree measures how lopsided evidence is across classes. High fairness means each class gets a fair shake.
Fairness degree is the variance of the alpha values (the evidence numbers) per class, penalizing imbalanced Dirichlet initialization.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: three interlocking moves
paras: Step 1 (Training-Based Guidance): During early training, the model makes mistakes. Some classes are harder to learn (rare ones often are). The paper records these mistakes by watching the model's confidence across training epochs. Classes the model got wrong early are flagged as high-priority. When the model constructs its Dirichlet distribution (the mathematical shape that defines evidence support), it now starts with guidance that says rare classes deserve a boost, because classes that the model struggles with early need extra support to keep up with common classes that are easy to learn. This guidance acts as a brake that prevents the model from starving rare classes during initialization.

Step 2 (Fairness Constraint): Even with a good starting guidance, the model can still slide back to old biases during training. So the paper adds a second constraint to the loss function: if evidence variance across classes gets too lopsided, training is nudged to correct it. The strength of this nudge gradually increases during training, so the model is not jerked around early on when it is still learning to extract evidence from the raw data, because imposing fairness too hard from the start would prevent the model from learning the basic task of extracting any evidence at all.

Step 3 (Opinion Alignment): Different views may have different biases. One view might over-support a common class; another might under-support it. The paper measures disagreement (dissonance) between pairs of views and adds a penalty if views are too far apart. This encourages the model to synthesize a consistent multi-view opinion instead of just averaging conflicting signals.

stages.s: Training-based guidance: boost rare classes based on early mistakes because classes that fail early need extra support

math.h2: The equation and what it means
math.words: Loss equals accuracy loss plus lambda times fairness degree, where fairness degree is the variance of evidence per class
symbols: standard accuracy loss, measures how wrong predictions are
a weight that starts at 0 and grows to 1, controlling how much fairness matters
fairness degree: variance of evidence allocations across classes

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose we have 3 classes: A (rare), B (medium), C (common).
Raw evidence from a view: A=2, B=5, C=10. Variance (spread) = 13.3.
Early epoch: lambda=0. Loss = L_ace only. Model freely assigns 2, 5, 10.
Mid epoch: lambda=0.5. Loss = L_ace + 0.5 * 13.3 = L_ace + 6.65. Now lopsidedness costs.
Late epoch: lambda=1.0. Loss = L_ace + 1.0 * 13.3. Maximum pressure to balance.
Model learns to produce more like A=6, B=7, C=9 (variance=1.3) to lower the penalty.

math.note: The gradual increase in lambda allows the model to first learn what each view contains, then refine allocations to be fair, because if fairness is imposed too hard early, the model cannot distinguish classes reliably in the first place.

bars.h2: The payoff: prediction and uncertainty both improve

charts.title: Without fairness (naive)
charts.note: Model is confident where it should not be, silent where it should say help, because without fairness enforcement, the model learns that common classes are easy and rare classes are too hard to bother with.

charts.title: With FAML (this paper)
charts.note: Slight trade-off on easy cases to gain big wins on hard cases and honest uncertainty.

items.html: If lambda ramps up too fast, the model is yanked toward fairness before it has learned the basic task. If too slow, fairness never kicks in. The paper uses a gradual schedule but real data may need tuning.

If a class has only one or two examples, fairness constraints can make the model dream up evidence that does not match the real data. Fairness is not the same as accuracy when data is extremely scarce.
If two views are mostly copies of each other (e.g., two hospital reports from the same patient records), the opinion alignment constraint can force artificial agreement and hide real disagreement.
The method works best when classes are moderately imbalanced (1:10 ratio or so) and views carry different real information. Monitor fairness and accuracy together during training.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Create a simple three-view dataset where one class has 200 examples and another has 20. Train a standard evidential model and then train FAML. Plot the evidence distributions (how tall the stacks are for each class). In the standard model, the rare class should have visibly smaller evidence stacks and lower confidence. In FAML, the stacks should be closer in height, and when the rare class is mislabeled, the model should admit uncertainty instead of staying confident.
demo.closing: The demo must show that FAML shrinks the gap between evidence allocated to the most-supported and least-supported classes, making the model honest about rare things.
